records.title: Lesotho Highlands Phase II construction and the path to water delivery
aliases: Lesotho Highlands Water Project Phase II
records.scope: The integrated Lesotho Highlands Water Project Phase II development, including Polihali dam and its transfer tunnel, counted once. Its component contracts and bridges are not additional projects; Phase I remains a separate historical system.
records.answer: Phase II remains under construction. Reported progress and a July 2027 impoundment target do not yet establish accepted water-transfer service or completed resettlement.
records.stage: Under construction; government and implementing-authority progress accounts

identity_decision.rationale: One named, integrated bilateral water-development project, absent from the retained project inventory. Dam, tunnel and related access works are components, not separately counted children. Mokhotlong is a distinct administrative place rather than a second project identity.

timeline.event: LHDA records approval of the Phase II compensation policy.
LHDA's June-indexed construction note distinguishes rockfill from whole-dam progress.
Government publishes its later construction and tunnel oversight account.

sections.heading: An integrated project with several responsible institutions
sections.text: The September government account assigns implementation to LHDA, financing to South Africa's Trans-Caledon Tunnel Authority and bilateral oversight to the Lesotho Highlands Water Commission. It reports overall construction at 56.7 percent and targets impoundment in July 2027. The institutional split matters: a contractor's progress report, a financing commitment and an acceptance decision answer different questions. Following the integrated development should not erase the separate obligations that connect its dam, tunnel and eventual transfer service.

sections.heading: Rockfill progress is not whole-dam completion
sections.text: LHDA's June-indexed note reports 9.1 million cubic metres of rock placed, around 65 percent of rockfill, against 45 percent completion for the dam overall. Intake, spillway, outlet and concrete-face work were still advancing. The two percentages describe different scopes, not competing estimates of one quantity. Elevation 2020 is a construction level, not a publication year. Comparing later progress requires the same work package and denominator; otherwise a large earthworks percentage can conceal unfinished systems needed to retain and release water safely.

sections.heading: The transfer tunnel remains a separate constraint
sections.text: The September account puts the 38-kilometre tunnel package at 58 percent overall while describing geological difficulties slowing the tunnel-boring machines. Package completion is not the percentage of a continuous waterway excavated or accepted. A reservoir can reach a visible milestone while its connecting works still control usable service. The next construction comparison therefore needs segment-level progress, remaining interfaces and an updated critical path, rather than applying the package percentage to every metre of tunnel.

sections.heading: Replacement housing is one part of resettlement
sections.text: LHDA's June housing note describes construction across replacement villages and a programme expected to finish in 2027. It does not turn houses under construction into completed household moves. Relocation combines buildings with usable services, access and the practical ability to resume everyday life. The linked Mokhotlong account follows those local questions separately. Keeping them alongside the engineering schedule makes it possible to ask whether a reservoir milestone and the affected communities' readiness are advancing together, without treating either as proof of the other.

sections.heading: Compensation requires more than an approved framework
sections.text: LHDA's overview records approval of a compensation policy in August 2016 and describes claims involving assets and relocation. It also discusses disputes and missing documentation affecting some payments. A policy establishes the framework for handling a claim; it does not establish that each claimant has received a satisfactory remedy. The operational account needs completed payments and unresolved cases tied to the relevant eligibility decision. Older household estimates on an undated overview should not silently replace a later, differently scoped relocation register.

sections.heading: The transition to service needs its own evidence
sections.text: The decisive next stage is a dated chain from completed works through safe impoundment and accepted transfer operations to repeated deliveries. Flow measurements need a stated interval, location and operating condition, while local outcomes need household and community measures. Costs should retain their price basis and distinguish spending to date from final expenditure. This editorial test allows construction achievement to remain visible without using it as a substitute for reliable service. It also keeps the project accountable to the people living with its physical changes, not only to its distant water customers.

next_artifacts: Updated dam and tunnel schedules with package definitions, accepted work and remaining interfaces.
Dated impoundment and transfer acceptance records followed by measured water delivery over a stated interval.
Household relocation, compensation and livelihood follow-up with unresolved cases and geographic scope.

records.title: Mokhotlong District resettlement livelihoods and public services
records.scope: Mokhotlong District in Lesotho, not only Mokhotlong town and not the Polihali reservoir footprint. Project-affected villages are subsets of the district; district residents, relocated households and individual houses retain separate denominators.
records.answer: Mokhotlong's local account combines replacement housing, treatment-plant maintenance and livelihood activity. Construction and training are important steps, but household recovery and sustained services require their own measures.
records.stage: Dated district and community account; construction and social programmes remain distinct from measured outcomes

identity_decision.rationale: One named Lesotho administrative district, absent from the retained eligible-place inventory. The account distinguishes the district from its town and project-affected villages; none of those nested locations is counted again in this batch. LHWP Phase II remains a separate project identity.

timeline.event: The census records 100,442 residents in Mokhotlong District.
LHDA indexes its social-development visit and complaints-management training accounts.
LHDA indexes its update on replacement-village house construction.

sections.heading: The district is larger than the affected communities
sections.text: The 2016 census records 100,442 people in Mokhotlong District. That is a historical administrative population, not a present-day estimate and not the number of residents affected by Polihali. This geographic distinction is essential when comparing services: a town-level treatment facility, a village relocation programme and district-wide demographic change describe different populations. The place account keeps their names and boundaries attached rather than allowing a single project footprint to stand in for the entire district.

sections.heading: House construction and household relocation use different units
sections.text: The June housing note reports 45 houses under construction at Tloha-re-Bue and 13 at Masakong, alongside community facilities. It separately describes households being resettled and work at other villages. A house, a household and a completed move are not interchangeable units. Counting roofs can help explain physical progress, but a relocation account also needs occupancy, water, sanitation and access. Its comparisons should follow the same households over time, rather than treating each construction milestone as another completed social outcome.

sections.heading: Treatment-plant maintenance connects local and reservoir concerns
sections.text: LHDA's May-indexed board visit identifies maintenance and long-term sustainability concerns at the WASCO sewer treatment plant in Mokhotlong. Wastewater management matters to local services and to water entering the future reservoir system. The account gives a concrete dependency to follow: sustained operation of a named facility, not simply the presence of infrastructure. Maintenance funding, responsible operators and dated treatment results would show whether the service is working. The board's visit identifies concerns; it is not itself a compliance determination.

sections.heading: Livelihood activity needs a household outcome measure
sections.text: The same visit describes the Ramonakalali livelihood demonstration hub and its role in skills and income opportunities. A training or demonstration site can support recovery without establishing that displaced households have regained their previous living standards. The useful follow-up is participation linked to durable earnings, productive assets and household costs over time. This keeps programme activity visible while avoiding an assumption that every participant benefits equally, or that a new opportunity compensates for every loss associated with relocation.

sections.heading: Complaint handling needs a visible path to resolution
sections.text: LHDA's May complaints note describes training for community liaison staff and arrangements involving local leadership and community structures. These are channels through which concerns can be raised and handled. Their effectiveness depends on what happens next: whether residents can access the process, receive a response and obtain a reasoned disposition. Training attendance alone does not answer those questions. A useful public series would separate new, unresolved and resolved complaints and retain the subject of each case without exposing private household information.

sections.heading: Follow the same people and services through the transition
sections.text: The strongest local account would connect a stable household cohort to completed moves, service continuity and livelihood changes, with clear consent and privacy safeguards. District statistics should remain a separate context series. It should also track the named public facilities serving both relocated and established residents, including maintenance responsibilities and recurring operating costs. These are editorial measurement priorities, not claims that the outcomes have already occurred. They make gains and unresolved burdens visible together and prevent a regional construction total from becoming an unsupported account of community recovery.

next_artifacts: A dated, privacy-preserving relocation and occupancy account with consistent household definitions.
Mokhotlong treatment-plant maintenance actions and operating results with periods and responsible institutions.
Livelihood and grievance follow-up distinguishing participation, unresolved cases and sustained household outcomes.

records.title: Cape Town municipal water security and household services
aliases: City of Cape Town Metropolitan Municipality
records.scope: The City of Cape Town Metropolitan Municipality in South Africa. The Western Cape province and the wider Western Cape Water Supply System are not the same geography; linked supply projects and individual suburbs add no further identities in this batch.
records.answer: Cape Town announced Level 1 restrictions on November 16 for a December 1 start. Its longer-term supply programme remains a delivery plan, while household access and service reliability require local measures beyond dam storage.
records.stage: Municipal water-service account; future restrictions announced and supply investments at different stages

identity_decision.rationale: One named metropolitan municipality, absent from the retained eligible-place inventory. The broader water-supply system is a physical dependency, not a second name for the municipal boundary. Programme components and suburbs are not separately counted projects or places here.

timeline.event: The City releases findings from its February to October 2024 household survey.
The City describes supply-programme progress and implementation delays.
The City announces restrictions effective December 1, after this article's inspection date.

sections.heading: A municipal service depends on a wider water system
sections.text: The government directory identifies the City of Cape Town as a metropolitan municipality. Its Water Outlook says the wider Western Cape Water Supply System provides more than 95 percent of the city's supply. Administrative responsibility and physical supply therefore have different boundaries. A regional storage measure can explain a common constraint, but cannot describe every municipal service or neighbourhood experience. This dossier follows the municipality while retaining the broader system as a dependency, without counting each reservoir or suburb as another place.

sections.heading: New supply has a schedule and implementation risks
sections.text: The City's August update describes a programme expected to add roughly 300 million litres per day of peak capacity by 2036. It also identifies delays and constraints, including financing and procurement for the Berg River–Voëlvlei scheme and uncertainty around the proposed Paarden Eiland desalination location. A programme total combines projects at different stages. It should not be added to present supply as though every component were already commissioned, nor treated as an annual volume without accounting for how often each source can operate.

sections.heading: The November announcement has a later effective date
sections.text: On November 16, the City announced Level 1 restrictions starting December 1 and called for at least ten percent lower use. It reported collective consumption of 951 million litres per day against an 860-million-litre target. Those are the announcement's dated figures, not a continuously updated dashboard. The restrictions were not yet in force on this article's November 21 inspection date. This distinction preserves both the policy decision and the time residents and services have to prepare for its implementation.

sections.heading: Household evidence reveals a different service geography
sections.text: The City released its first city-wide household survey findings in September 2025, covering fieldwork from February to October 2024. The survey included more than 8,000 households across formal homes, informal settlements and backyard dwellings, with questions about services and vulnerability. That design offers a route to examine distribution rather than just municipal totals. The release alone does not supply a current water-access rate for any particular suburb. Such a comparison needs the underlying measure, sample and dwelling-type definitions attached to each result.

sections.heading: Existing infrastructure also needs sustained investment
sections.text: The Water Outlook sets out a refurbishment programme for bulk assets and links operational stability to resource allocation, prioritisation and sustained institutional commitment. Supply expansion is therefore only one side of resilience; existing equipment must continue to work while new capacity is delivered. The household perspective adds another test: whether maintenance and demand management preserve usable service where people live. An investment requirement is a plan for work, not evidence that interruptions, losses or unequal access have already declined.

sections.heading: Connect delivery to repeated and fairly distributed service
sections.text: A stronger operating account would pair commissioned capacity and actual production with interruptions, water quality, affordability and access by neighbourhood and dwelling type. The series should preserve reporting periods and explain changes in boundaries or methods before comparing years. Restriction implementation and its effects should be assessed after the effective date, separately from the decision to impose it. These editorial priorities make it possible to evaluate both system security and distribution: more water entering the network does not automatically establish that every household receives a reliable and affordable service.

next_artifacts: Restriction implementation and measured demand after December 1, with the observation period explicit.
Named supply-project commissioning and actual production, retaining delays and operating limitations.
Household and neighbourhood service measures with sample definitions, affordability and interruption data.
